title: Replacing a push-fit soil pipe collar
subtitle: Remove the perished rubber collar from a push-fit soil pipe joint and fit a new collar to restore the seal against odour and leakage
excerpt: How to replace the rubber collar inside a push-fit soil pipe joint. Covers preparing the area, pulling the joint apart, removing the old collar, cleaning the socket, fitting the new collar, and pushing the joint home.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK trade plumbing practice for soil and waste pipework.

glossaryTerms.definition: The large-diameter pipe, typically 100 to 110 mm, that carries foul waste from toilet pans and urinals to the drain or sewer. In older construction it is cast iron; in modern buildings it is uPVC. The soil pipe connects to the sewer at ground level and vents through the roof to allow gases to escape.

The rubber ring seal seated in a groove inside the socket end of a push-fit soil pipe fitting. When the spigot end of the next pipe section is pushed home, the collar compresses to form a watertight and gas-tight seal. Over time, rubber collars perish, harden, and lose their sealing capability, allowing odours and occasional drips.

content.text: joint seals the two sections together. When a collar perishes, odour or drips appear at the joint. Replacing it takes under 30 minutes and needs no specialist tools. BEGINNER: no plumbing connections are broken.
Prepare the area and support the pipe

Clear the area around the joint and place a bucket or container below to catch any residual water in the pipe. If the soil pipe runs through a duct or boxing, the affected section of the access panel must be removed. If the pipe is fastened to the wall with a pipe clip directly at the joint, loosen the clip before trying to separate the joint.

Pull the spigot end of the downstream pipe section out of the socket while twisting slightly. On a horizontal run this is usually straightforward by hand; on a vertical run it may require gripping the pipe with both hands and pulling down against the socket. Lay the separated spigot end aside.
Remove the old collar and clean the socket

Work the old collar out of the seating groove in the socket using a finger or the handle of the utility knife. The collar will be hard and brittle if it has perished. Clean out the groove with a dry cloth to remove any debris or deposits. Wipe the inside of the socket and the spigot end with a damp cloth and allow to dry.
Fit the new collar and push home

Lubricate the new collar with a small amount of petroleum jelly or silicone grease on the inner face. Press it into the seating groove in the socket, working around the full circumference so it is evenly seated. Apply a thin smear of the same lubricant to the spigot end of the downstream pipe. Push the spigot firmly and steadily into the socket until it reaches the insertion depth mark or the socket stops. Twist slightly while pushing to help the collar seat.

attrs.symptom: Collar rolls out of the groove when the spigot is pushed in
attrs.cause: The collar was not evenly seated in the groove before insertion, or insufficient lubrication allowed the collar to drag.
attrs.fix: Pull the joint apart and reseat the collar carefully all around the groove. Apply lubricant to both the collar inner face and the spigot end.

attrs.symptom: Joint still drips after the collar is replaced
attrs.cause: The spigot end was not pushed far enough into the socket, or the spigot pipe is cracked or damaged.
attrs.fix: Check the insertion depth: the spigot end should be fully home. Inspect the spigot surface for cracks or ridges and replace the pipe section if damaged.
